newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Downgrade a blow to Union Bank of Switzerland prestige.
newsitem.headline: Downgrade a blow to Union Bank of Switzerland prestige.

text.p: A downgrading of Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) is a further blow to the bank's prestige, which has been eroded by an employee shredding historical documents from the Nazi era, analysts said.
But apart from its prestige, analysts said UBS would not suffer any real financial effect from Standard & Poor's lowering of its long-term rating of the bank to double-A from triple-A.
Although UBS regretted the decision by S&P, a spokeswoman said the move was expected and UBS was still among the leading banks in the world.
"Of course it is regretable, but we are still on the top of the leading banks in the world," a UBS spokeswoman said.
S&P had put UBS on creditwatch with negative implications on November 26 on concern over the quality of the assets in its Swiss portfolio.
Earlier that month UBS had announced it would record a 1996 loss of some 500 million francs ($363.1 million) due to loan-loss provisions.
The UBS spokeswoman noted that UBS chief executive Mathis Cabiallavetta had said the possible downgrade actually presented the bank with an incentive to try to solve its problems with domestic loans.
Analysts said S&P's move would hardly have any effect on UBS's refinancing costs as the bank was still very highly capitalised and presented no financing risk.
"UBS has a very high capital ratio so it's unlikely to suffer," said James Alexander of Kleinwort Benson.
"The most important effect is on its prestige," he added, noting that UBS had used the triple-A rating in its advertising in the past.
UBS said it had stopped using the triple-A rating in its advertising a few years ago.
"UBS is still a first class bank and is practically a zero credit risk," said Madeleine Hofmann of Credit Suisse, noting the bank is actually overcapitalised.

Ratings agencies like S&P and Moody's Investors Service have been downgrading banks over the last few years and the only bank that is still triple-A rated by both agencies is Dutch Rabobank Netherland BV, a cooperative.
Moody's still gives UBS its highest rating, Aaa.
Last December Moody's downgraded Germany's Deutsche Bank AG to AA1 from AAA, leaving UBS as the only bank, apart from Rabobank, that was triple-rated by both agencies, analysts said.
Alexander said S&P's downgrade may actually have a positive outcome because UBS will no longer have to keep up its high capital ratio to protect the triple-A rating.
"Now they could pay some money back to shareholders," Alexander said.
